query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of the HfNbTaTiZr refractory HEA is primarily controlled by the interplay between cold‐work induced dislocation networks (and their associated residual internal stresses) and the thermal expansion mismatch that develops when nano‐scale precipitates form during aging (600–800 °C). This coupling produces internal stresses that simultaneously stiffen the matrix (raising microhardness and elastic moduli at ambient and intermediate temperatures) and modify high‐temperature dislocation mobility (affecting tensile creep at ~1250 °C).
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr alloy in the as‐cast, single BCC phase state before any thermo‐mechanical processing.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled cold rolling to generate high dislocation densities followed by aging at 600–800 °C to initiate fine precipitate formation, then compare with a set of samples that receive an additional stress‐relief annealing (homogenization) step to remove internal residual stresses.
generation.conditions: Test the alloy under (a) elastic modulus measurements from room temperature up to ~1100 K, (b) tensile creep tests at 1250 °C, and (c) microhardness evaluations after cold rolling versus after aging without and with stress-relief annealing. The aging treatment is conducted in the 600–800 °C range, while the creep and elastic tests are performed within the reported boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: The high density of cold‐work-induced dislocations and the development of nano‐scale precipitates (with a different thermal expansion coefficient than the matrix) that together create residual internal stresses.
generation.mechanism: Cold rolling produces a substantial dislocation network that remains as stored energy and introduces lattice distortions. Subsequent aging promotes fine precipitate formation which, due to its lower lattice constant and different thermal expansion‐coefficient from the parent BCC phase, creates a mismatch that induces thermal stresses. These internal stresses enhance the elastic modulus and microhardness at lower temperatures and alter the kinetics of dislocation motion (e.g., pinning and climb) under high-temperature (1250 °C) creep conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline sample that has undergone stress-relief annealing (thereby largely relieving internal stresses), the non–stress-relieved cold-rolled and aged alloy is predicted to show a higher yield strength, increased microhardness and elastic modulus at room to intermediate temperatures, and a modified (likely lower) creep rate at 1250 °C because of stronger dislocation pinning. In other words, the residual stresses from dislocations and precipitate-induced thermal expansion mismatch act to stiffen the alloy and change its creep response.
generation.baseline: Samples that are processed by cold rolling and aging but then subjected to an additional stress-relief anneal to remove the enhanced internal stresses.
generation.boundary: Temperature boundaries include ambient (~293 K) to ~1100 K for elastic moduli measurements, aging conducted between 600–800 °C, and tensile creep testing at approximately 1250 °C. The response is measured in terms of yield strength, hardness, elastic modulus, and creep rate in these regimes.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative contributions of dislocation density versus precipitate-induced mismatch are not yet established, and potential microstructural heterogeneities or minor oxidation effects at high temperatures could also influence the results.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples: one set undergoes cold rolling and aging (600–800 °C) with no further treatment, while the second set receives an additional homogenizing (stress-relief) anneal to largely remove the cold-work stored energy and associated residual stresses. Measure and compare their elastic moduli (from 293 to 1100 K), microhardness, and high-temperature tensile creep behavior (at 1250 °C).
measurements: Elastic modulus across the temperature range (293–1100 K)
Yield strength and creep rate from high-temperature tensile tests at 1250 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the removal of residual stresses via stress-relief annealing does not produce a significant reduction in elastic modulus, microhardness, and yield strength (or does not alter the high-temperature creep rate) compared to the non-annealed, cold-rolled and aged samples, then the hypothesis that internal residual stresses (from dislocation networks and thermal expansion mismatch) govern the unified behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). AbstractTitanium-rich metastable medium-entropy alloys, designed for low elastic moduli, sacrifice strength. However, enhancing their mechanical strength is crucial for bio-implant applications. This study aims to enhance the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of a metastable Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 medium-entropy alloy using various treatments, including cold rolling (at 50% and 75% reduction) and precipitation hardening (at room temperature, 150 °C, 350 °C, 550 °C, and 750 °C). The results showed that the alloy underwent a stress-induced martensitic transformation during the rolling process. Notably, the α phase was precipitated in the β grain boundaries after 30 days of precipitation hardening at room temperature. The yield strengths of the alloy increased by 51% and 281.9% after room-temperature precipitation and 75% cold rolling, respectively. In potentiodynamic corrosion tests conducted in phosphate-buffered saline solution, the pitting potentials of the alloy treated using various conditions were higher than 1.8 V, and no pitting holes were observed on the surface of the alloys. cited_evidence.text: Overall, this comprehensive study provides evidence for the unique elastic and plastic deformation behavior of the single BCC solid-solution phase refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using in situ neutron experiments coupled with theoretical calculations. The results of the ND and characterization of the microstructure show the excellent BCC single-phase stability up to 900°C. Furthermore, the present alloy has the high yield strength and excellent plasticity at RT and softening resistance at elevated temperatures. The lattice strain evolution results show the distinctive elastic deformation behavior as an elastic isotropy at RT and less temperature dependency in the elastic anisotropic deformation behavior than conventional metallic materials at elevated temperatures. The single-crystal elastic moduli are obtained from the in situ ND data coupled with the Kroner model approach, showing excellent agreement with the experimental values determined from RUS measurements and first-principles calculations.
